To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the practice of life cycle assessment (in this case in the forest product industry in Sweden) can be understood as a result of individual preferences and chance.
the practice of LCA in the forest product industry is shaped by individual preferences and by chance events, rather than by ‘structural’ factors.

LCA practice in two companies in the same sector (forest products) and country (Sweden) was shaped more by individual and chance factors than by ‘structural’ conditions, and that this implies that LCA is a more interpretive phenomenon than has been put forth by previous research.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of life cycle assessment in industry.
the use of life cycle assessment ( LCA ) in industry.
the question of what motivates companies to use LCA and the implications of this question for the development of LCA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘the adoption of LCA is a complex phenomenon, and it is not easy to predict whether or not a company will adopt LCA, or when and how this will occur’.
LCA practice in this study has been characterized by an interpretive understanding.
LCA practice in these two companies is not determined by the ‘structural’ conditions of sector and location, but rather by the individual preferences of the practitioners and chance events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structural understanding of LCA is too simple and does not take into account the importance of interpretation.
we have shown how LCA can be used in practice, and that LCA practice can be understood as a social process.
the LCA practice of a company is a result of an interaction between the structural conditions of the company and the individual preferences of the LCA-practitioner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structural conditions of location and sector are less important than the interpretive understanding of life cycle assessment (i.e., how LCA is understood by the people involved).
LCA practice can be understood as a social practice.

LCA practice should be understood in a more interpretive way, and that this understanding has implications for practitioners, organizations promoting the uptake of LCA in companies, as well as for researchers.
